clinicalPearls: A common hair-shaft abnormality in which small greyish-white nodes along the shaft represent sites of cortical fracture, giving hair that breaks easily
Under the microscope the nodes resemble the ends of two brushes or brooms pushed together at the fracture point, the classic paintbrush appearance
It may be proximal, distal or localised, and distal trichorrhexis nodosa from cumulative cosmetic and physical trauma such as heat, bleaching and brushing is the commonest form

Acquired forms follow physical or chemical trauma to otherwise normal or inherently weakened hair, whereas congenital forms accompany metabolic disorders such as argininosuccinic aciduria and other hair-shaft syndromes
Trichoscopy shows the nodes and transverse fractures with brush-like broken ends
Proximal trichorrhexis nodosa is more common in afro-textured hair and with certain metabolic conditions
Management focuses on eliminating traumatic hair practices and treating any underlying disorder, and hair usually recovers once trauma stops in acquired cases
reference.pathophysiology: Trichorrhexis nodosa arises when the protective cuticle is disrupted, exposing the cortex, whose fibres then splay apart to form the characteristic nodes and fracture transversely. It may reflect an inherent weakness of the shaft, as in inherited metabolic disorders affecting keratin sulphur content or amino-acid metabolism, or, more often, cumulative physical and chemical trauma from grooming, heat and cosmetic processing acting on normal or vulnerable hair. The result is localised structural failure and breakage.
additionalDifferentials: Pili torti, with twisting but no nodes
Other causes of hair fragility and breakage
additionalInvestigations: Light microscopy of the shaft showing paired brush-like fracture ends at the nodes
Trichoscopy demonstrating nodes and transverse fractures
Metabolic screening, for example for argininosuccinic aciduria, where a congenital cause is suspected
Assessment for associated hair-shaft syndromes or systemic disease
redFlags: Widespread congenital fragility suggesting an underlying metabolic or genetic disorder
Failure to improve despite stopping trauma, prompting a search for an inherent shaft defect
reference.prognosis: Acquired distal trichorrhexis nodosa usually recovers once traumatic practices cease, whereas congenital or metabolic-associated forms depend on the underlying disorder and may be more persistent.
pitfalls: Attributing breakage to hair loss rather than a shaft defect and so missing the true cause
Overlooking an underlying metabolic disorder in congenital cases
Not taking a full cosmetic and grooming history in acquired disease
Failing to examine the shaft microscopically to confirm the diagnosis
management: Remove the causative mechanical and chemical trauma by stopping heat styling, bleaching, chemical relaxing and vigorous brushing, which is the mainstay for the common acquired distal form
Adopt gentle hair-care measures with mild shampoos, conditioners and low-tension styling to minimise cortical fracture and allow the shaft to recover
Investigate and treat an underlying metabolic disorder in congenital cases, such as dietary and substrate management of argininosuccinic aciduria under a metabolic team
Identify and correct associated systemic contributors such as iron deficiency and hypothyroidism
Monitor for regrowth of intact hair after harmful practices cease, which confirms the acquired mechanism
Refer to clinical genetics or metabolic medicine when a congenital hair-shaft or amino-acid disorder is suspected
